Financial planning · Inflation sequence · Visual planning guide

The same ten-year inflation total can require different retirement capital

Five charts reverse the order of two invented inflation blocks, then trace spending requests, portfolio balances, funding requirements and any unmet spending.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Reverse two inflation blocks while preserving the same ten-year price increase

Interactive planning lab

Additional opening capital: A-first minus B-first$28,342.15
Remaining capital at year ten, block A first$403,919.34
Unfunded spending requests: A-first / B-first0 / 0 CAD

Two invented ten-year inflation sequences contain exactly the same annual rates in opposite order. Block A is 8% for 3 years; block B is 2% for 7 years. The first spending request is made immediately at the start of year one, before any price increase or investment return. Later requests reflect the previous year-end price index. Each requested amount can use only available capital; any gap stays unfunded and is never borrowed automatically. The constant nominal return then applies to remaining capital, followed by that year’s inflation update for the next year. Thus the tenth inflation update affects closing purchasing power but no eleventh spending request is included. Opening-capital requirements discount all ten requested start-of-year withdrawals at the selected constant nominal return. They are deterministic funding identities, not safe-withdrawal recommendations or probabilities. No tax, fees, pensions, consumption substitution or additional income is modeled.

The central idea

A closing price level does not reveal when the price increases arrived. Earlier increases can affect more withdrawals, even when the investment return and final price level match.

01

Hold the inflation factors constant and change only their order

The first chart draws two price paths. In the original example, one has three years of 8% inflation followed by seven years of 2%. The other reverses exactly those ten annual factors. Both finish with the same price level: approximately 144.7 when the starting index is 100.

The rates are invented. They are not a replay of Canadian CPI, an estimate of future prices or probabilities assigned to a retirement scenario. Their purpose is to hold the total compounded increase constant while changing when it occurs.

The two blocks remain labelled A and B when inputs change. If block A is entered below block B, the first path no longer represents higher inflation arriving early. If both rates are equal, the paths coincide. The labels describe order rather than promising which sequence is more difficult.

02

Every spending request needs a price observation and a payment date

The first annual withdrawal request is made immediately at the start of year one, before any modeled inflation or investment return. The next year’s request follows the price level after year one. Each later request uses the preceding year-end price index to maintain the same selected spending basket.

The second chart shows these requested nominal amounts. A price increase early in the horizon affects several later requests. A price increase at the very end cannot change an earlier bill that has already been requested.

This convention also explains the tenth inflation update. It determines the closing year-ten price level and purchasing power, but an eleventh withdrawal is outside the ten-year horizon. The year-ten request uses the first nine price increases. Matching closing indices therefore does not require the ten withdrawal amounts or their sum to match.

03

Keep returns identical to isolate the inflation-spending channel

The third chart gives both withdrawal paths the same initial capital and the same constant nominal investment return. The original example starts with CAD 500,000, requests CAD 25,000 immediately, and uses an assumed 5% effective nominal return every year.

Each request first uses the capital available at the start of that year. The remaining capital then earns the selected return. The tool records any amount that cannot be funded; it does not borrow automatically or show a negative investment account.

Under the original assumptions, the A-first path requests about CAD 315,286 across the decade and ends with about CAD 403,919. The reversed path requests about CAD 279,084 and ends with about CAD 450,086. Both original examples fund all ten requests. The difference combines extra spending with the growth forgone on earlier withdrawals; it is not an investment-performance difference.

The no-spending line is a control. It removes all withdrawal requests and therefore produces one common investment path. It is not a retirement lifestyle that a household can adopt without a separate source of income.

04

Discount every requested withdrawal from its actual timing

The fourth chart calculates the opening capital required to fund the ten requests under the selected constant return, ending with no capital requirement beyond the horizon. The first request is immediate and is not discounted. The request at the start of year two is discounted one year, and so on.

The equation is required opening capital = Σ requested spending in year t ÷ (1 + nominal return)t − 1 for years one through ten. These cash-flow dates must agree with the portfolio recurrence; using year-end discounting would answer a different question.

In the original example, the requirements are approximately CAD 252,029 with block A first and CAD 223,686 with block B first. The difference is approximately CAD 28,342. A third bar holds the initial spending request and nominal return constant while removing all price increases, providing a separate inflation control.

This is an arithmetic funding identity for ten known requests and one certain return assumption. It is not a recommended reserve, a safe withdrawal rate or a statement that retirement ends after ten years.

05

Read unmet spending beside the remaining portfolio

The final chart separates requested spending into amounts funded and left unfunded. A lower funded total can mean that the household could not meet its needs. It should not be praised as a more efficient spending strategy without reading the unfunded segment.

Try reducing initial capital. The opening-capital requirement bars do not change because they depend on the requested spending path and return. The actual portfolio path and unmet requests do change. Later returns cannot retroactively finance an earlier request that lacked capital.

A real retirement plan would also include pensions, tax, fees, changing spending quantities, benefit indexation, cash timing and uncertain returns. Price increases may differ by category, and households may adjust discretionary spending. This example isolates one channel to make its effect visible.

  1. Keep a record of whether values are nominal or in today’s purchasing power.
  2. Specify when each withdrawal happens.
  3. Test earlier as well as later inflation pressure.
  4. Show any spending cuts or unmet requests beside capital balances.
  5. Extend the horizon and add other resources before treating the exercise as a retirement plan.

The useful question is how price changes reach the budget through time, rather than only which index value appears at the finish.
